title: A mountain humbled
hookLine: had We sent this Qur'an on a mountain, you'd see it humbled and split (59:21)

lines: AT THE FOOT OF A MOUNTAIN.
cards: A mountain doesn't move. Lean your whole weight on one and it won't notice. It was there before everyone you know was born, and it'll be there after.
Weather breaks on it. Centuries go past it. It's hard to imagine anything that could make a mountain tremble.
Surah Al-Hashr, in its closing verses, imagines exactly that. And what shakes the mountain isn't an earthquake. It's a book.

teach.b: Verse twenty-one. Pickthall: "If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah." Two words carry the picture.
Khashi'an, humbled, from the same root as khushu', the stillness of prayer we met a week ago.
And mutasaddi'an, split, cracking apart. The mountain bows, then breaks. Then the verse explains itself: such parables we strike for people, so that they may reflect.
The point lands on us. If this speech would humble a mountain, what is it doing to a human heart that hears it and stays the same? The Qur'an has shown a mountain like this before.
In Surah Al-A'raf, Musa asks to see God. He's told to look at the mountain: if it stays in place, you will see me.
When his Lord revealed himself to the mountain, it crumbled to dust, and Musa fell down senseless. And in Surah Al-Ahzab, God offers the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains.
They decline it, afraid of it, and the human being takes it on. The mountains in the Qur'an know their limits.
Here's the startling reversal: the hardest thing in the landscape trembles, while a person can hear the same words and feel nothing. The verse doesn't scold.

teach.h: A MIRROR: SO THAT THEY MAY REFLECT.
teach.b: It holds up the mountain like a mirror and leaves its hearers to reflect.

how: The last verses of Surah Al-Hashr, from this verse to the end, are often recited together, and many Muslims read 59:21 as a call to let the Qur'an soften the heart.

o: the prophet to whom the Qur'an itself was revealed
the prophet who built the Kaaba with his son
the prophet who asked to see God, and saw a mountain crumble

games.q: the mountain in the Qur'an — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says the Qur'an was actually sent down on a mountain
it's a parable: if it had been, the mountain would have been humbled and split.
the verse says such parables are struck so people may reflect
the point lands on the listener.
in Al-A'raf, the mountain crumbles when God reveals himself to it

games.q: you're Musa, asking to see God. you're told: look at the mountain; if it stays in its place, you'll see me. what happens?
o: the mountain stands, and Musa sees.
the mountain crumbles to dust, and Musa falls senseless.
games.why: the mountain crumbled, and Musa fell down. Al-Hashr's mountain, humbled by the Qur'an, echoes that scene.

practice: If you can see a hill, a tall building or even a big tree, stand and face it; if not, close your eyes and picture the largest mountain you've ever seen. Stand tall, feet planted, and feel how solid you are, and how solid it is.
If you pray, let your shoulders soften a little in humility before what's greater; if not, simply notice what it's like to be small next to something vast.

wordCard.voice: Musa: the prophet who asked to see God and watched the mountain crumble to dust, a mountain's trembling that Surah Al-Hashr names again. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: humbled, split apart. khashi'an shares a root with khushu', the stillness of prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the mountain would crumble. Words that heavy deserve a slow hearing. Day six hundred twenty, done.
